column4: Exactly the same pixel-art look, grain and muted dirty colours as the reference picture, but a new picture seen from the chair in front of a desk: an old 1990s laptop computer standing open on a scuffed motel desk, filling the frame, its lid upright and perfectly square to the viewer with no perspective on it, its edges parallel to the edges of the picture. A cheap wannabe of a classic grey-white notebook of the early nineties: pale warm platinum-grey plastic gone a little yellow, a chunky case with softly rounded corners, a wide bezel, thicker at the bottom, with one small embossed dark green pear badge in the middle of the bottom bezel and nothing written anywhere. The screen takes about two thirds of the picture's width and about three quarters of its height and must be one flat solid pure magenta #FF00FF rectangle with sharp straight edges, perfectly even, nothing on it. Under the lid the two hinges, then a narrow strip of the keyboard deck with the top row of dark grey keys along the bottom edge of the picture. Either side of the lid a dim shabby motel room behind the desk: a stained wallpaper wall, dark, the weak light of a lamp from the left. Grimy, silent, nobody there. No text, no letters, no logos other than the pear, no border, no watermark.

A row of 1990s pixel-art desktop icons for a classic Macintosh-like operating system, each drawn as if it were 32 by 32 pixels blown up: thick clean black outlines, light grey and white surfaces, a few muted colours, simple flat dithered shading, a soft three-quarter view, the icons standing apart from each other in one row with wide gaps, all the same size, each filling its place. Background must be flat solid pure magenta #FF00FF everywhere around them, no shadow on the background, no text, no letters, no numbers, no border, no watermark. Left to right, four icons: a small flat rectangular external hard disk box in light grey with one tiny green light; a ribbed grey metal waste bin with its lid on; the same waste bin with its lid pushed up and crumpled white paper sticking out; a plain closed file folder in dusty blue-grey with a tab.

Bottom row, left to right, four icons: a white sheet of paper with grey lines of writing and a black fountain pen lying across it; a small light grey pocket calculator with a narrow display and rows of little blank buttons; a square frame holding a four by four grid of small light grey blank square tiles with one tile missing in the bottom right corner; an open cardboard software box with a black floppy disk standing out of it.

First: a plain flat pear logo, a simple solid dark green pear shape with a short black stem and one small leaf, no shading, thick black outline. Second: the same pear, big and pale yellow-green, with a simple black line face drawn on it like a computer's cheerful start-up picture: two small dot eyes that are not quite level and a thin long smile that goes on a little too far, quiet and slightly wrong, not cartoonish.

A seamless tileable repeating pattern for the desktop of a 1990s computer, flat front view filling the whole square: staggered rows of tiny identical pear shapes, each pear only a few pixels big, in dull dark sage green on a slightly lighter dull sage green ground, checker dither between the two greens, low contrast, only three or four colours, crisp hand-pixelled look like an old operating system's desktop pattern, no perspective. No text, no border, no watermark, must tile seamlessly on all four edges.
